title: Robot Workshop
subtitle: How do robots receive information, decide, and act?
coreQuestion: Do robots use magic, or do sensors, programs, and action parts work together?
learningGoals: Recognize robots as input, decision, action, and feedback systems.
Know that cameras, microphones, buttons, and distance sensors can receive information.
Understand that wheels, lights, and robot arms are action or feedback parts.
misconceptions: Any toy with a screen or motion is a robot.

hero.title: Robot Workshop
hero.kicker: Human-Made Systems World · Input and Action
hero.lead: A robot first sees or hears, then follows rules, and finally acts.
hero.sceneExplanation: The main scene is a friendly robot workbench: inputs such as camera, microphone, button, and distance sensor on the left; a program-thinking cloud in the center; lights, wheels, and a robot arm as outputs on the right.
hero.childPrompt: Help the robot find what it receives first and what it does next.
hero.parentPrompt: Build system flow without over-personifying the robot.

classificationGroups.name: Receive information
classificationGroups.childExplanation: Sensors are like a robot’s eyes, ears, and buttons.
classificationGroups.parentNote: Use receiving information instead of complex hardware terms.
classificationGroups.misconception: Robots know the outside world without sensing.

classificationGroups.name: Decision rules
classificationGroups.childExplanation: A program tells the robot what to do in different situations.
classificationGroups.parentNote: Compare it to a task card or traffic rule.
classificationGroups.misconception: Robots freely think whatever they want.

classificationGroups.name: Take action
classificationGroups.childExplanation: Wheels, lights, and robot arms let a robot move or show a result.
classificationGroups.parentNote: No need to use the term actuator first.
classificationGroups.misconception: Lighting and moving are the same ability.

classificationGroups.name: Check and adjust
classificationGroups.childExplanation: After acting, a robot can check the result again.
classificationGroups.misconception: Robots only act once and never check.

representativeObjects.name: Camera
representativeObjects.childExplanation: A camera helps a robot see images.
representativeObjects.commonMisread: Thinking the camera is the brain.

representativeObjects.name: Microphone
representativeObjects.childExplanation: A microphone helps a robot hear sounds.

representativeObjects.name: Button
representativeObjects.childExplanation: A button can tell the robot a human choice.

representativeObjects.name: Distance sensor
representativeObjects.childExplanation: It helps a robot know whether something is close in front.
representativeObjects.commonMisread: Thinking it sees exactly like human eyes.

representativeObjects.name: Program rules
representativeObjects.childExplanation: A program is like task rules telling the robot what to do.

representativeObjects.name: Wheel
representativeObjects.childExplanation: Wheels let the robot move forward, backward, or turn.
representativeObjects.commonMisread: Thinking wheels alone make a robot.

representativeObjects.name: Light
representativeObjects.childExplanation: Lights can show the robot’s current state.

representativeObjects.name: Robot arm
representativeObjects.childExplanation: A robot arm can reach, grab, or push things.
representativeObjects.commonMisread: Thinking it works exactly like a human hand.

mechanism.title: How does a robot complete a task?

steps.childExplanation: A camera, microphone, button, or sensor receives information first.
The robot gives the information to the program to see what is happening.
The program follows task rules to decide the next step.
steps.parentNote: Avoid saying the robot freely thinks.

steps.childExplanation: Wheels, lights, or a robot arm start working.
The robot can check the result and adjust if needed.
The distance sensor notices something in front.
The program says: if too close, stop.
The wheels stop turning so the robot does not bump into it.

a.name: Sensor
points: camera, microphone, and button can be inputs

b.name: Action part
points: turns a decision into a result

comparePairs.title: Program vs Magic

a.name: Program
points: same input often gives same action

comparePairs.childConclusion: Robots work through programs and parts, not magic.

comparePairs.title: Robot vs Remote toy
comparePairs.childConclusion: Moving is not enough; sensing and rule-based action matter.

clickTasks.title: What is the order of a robot task?
clickTasks.prompt: Tap from receiving information to acting.
clickTasks.wrongHint: A robot must know what happened before it acts.
clickTasks.successCopy: You arranged the basic robot workflow!

clickTasks.title: Find: which parts receive information?
clickTasks.prompt: Find the parts that can receive outside information.
clickTasks.wrongHint: Is it knowing information or doing an action?
clickTasks.successCopy: Correct! These parts help the robot receive information.

clickTasks.title: What do robots not rely on?

wrongHints.sensors-program: Sensors and programs are key to robot work.
wrongHints.wheels-arm: Wheels and arms help robots act.

clickTasks.successCopy: Right! Robots do not work by magic.

speakTemplates: A robot first uses ____ to receive information.
A program is like ____ that tells the robot what to do.
Wheels and robot arms are ____ parts.
parentTips: Use home examples like robot vacuums, automatic doors, or voice lights.
Avoid saying robots truly understand everything; say they process information by rules.
If interested, ask the child to draw an input-decision-action flow.

intro: Robots do not work by magic.
They receive information, follow program rules, and act with wheels, lights, or robot arms.
keyFacts: Sensors help robots receive outside information.
Programs are like task rules for deciding the next step.
Action parts let robots move, light up, grab, or make sounds.
copy.explainPrompt: Can you describe a robot process: see, decide, and move?

acceptanceCriteria: The child can name input, decision, and action.
The child can distinguish sensors from action parts.
The child can explain robot work without using magic.
